title: A good campaign knows when the cost of persuasion has become the cost of the product.
dek: Claude C. Hopkins's Chapter 10 is a lesson in commercial judgment: some educational or distribution tasks may be possible, but their cost can outrun the value of the result. Advertising improves when the project is measured against a known return.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Ambition is not a budget. Hopkins asks the advertiser to weigh the cost of changing behavior, educating a market, or reaching a prospect against the result that can reasonably be expected.

canon.heading: Hopkins: measure the cost of making a sale before you mistake effort for strategy.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 10, "Things Too Costly," from Claude C. Hopkins's Scientific Advertising, on PDF pages 31-33. Hopkins is not arguing for timid advertising; he is arguing that every ambitious project needs a cost-and-result test.
canon.readerIntro: Read the chapter as a filter for expensive persuasion. Mark where Hopkins distinguishes what can be done from what is worth doing, where he prices the difficulty of changing habits or teaching a market, and where he insists that the method be judged by a known scale of cost and result.

blocks.label: 01 / Possible is not the same as profitable
paragraphs: Hopkins begins with a useful separation: advertising can attempt many things, but the fact that an effort is possible does not make it commercially sound.
The apprentice question is therefore not only Can we make this campaign? It is What result would justify its cost, and what evidence would tell us before we spend too much?

blocks.label: 02 / Changing habits carries a hidden bill
paragraphs: When an offer requires people to learn a new behavior, the advertiser is paying for education before the product can receive its ordinary demand.

That cost may be justified, but it should be visible in the plan. A new category, unfamiliar mechanism, or difficult conversion path needs a budget that matches the work of changing the prospect's assumptions.

blocks.label: 03 / Compare projects on the same commercial scale
paragraphs: Hopkins's standard is comparative. One project may produce a result at a fraction of the cost of another, even when both appear equally attractive in a meeting.
This is an early unit-economics discipline: estimate the cost of reaching and converting the prospect, then let measured response decide which method deserves more investment.

blocks.label: 04 / Education must eventually hand off to desire
paragraphs: The chapter's warning is especially sharp when advertising tries to explain a broad subject instead of selling a concrete offer. Information consumes attention, time, and money; it needs a clear path to action.
A campaign should know what the reader is being taught, why that knowledge changes the choice, and where the product becomes the economical next step.

blocks.label: 05 / The apprentice test
paragraphs: List one current initiative that depends on market education, behavior change, or a costly distribution route. Write down the expected result and the earliest signal that would justify continuing.
If the project has no stop point, comparison, or known return, it may be asking enthusiasm to do the work of judgment.

passageAnchors: weighed and determined by a known scale of cost and result
closeReading: Which kinds of advertising work does Hopkins consider possible but too expensive?
Why does changing a habit cost more than explaining a product?
Where does Hopkins compare the cost of result across different offers or audiences?
What is the known scale of cost and result for one project you are currently running?
What early signal would tell you that an ambitious educational campaign should be stopped or narrowed?

principle.heading: A strategy earns its ambition by naming the cost of the result.
principle.body: Hopkins's lesson is not to avoid difficult markets. It is to price the difficulty honestly. The advertiser who knows what must be taught, what behavior must change, and what result can repay the work has a basis for choosing methods instead of merely admiring possibilities.
principle.example: A SaaS company can spend months teaching a new reporting category, or begin with teams already searching for a narrower reporting problem. The second route may not be as grand, but it gives the company a known cost per qualified conversation and a faster test of whether the promise is wanted.
principle.practice: Choose one current campaign or growth initiative. Estimate its cost to reach, educate, and convert one qualified customer. Write the result that would justify the effort and the earliest evidence that the estimate is wrong.

fieldNotes.title: Apple turns the watch into a daily interpretation layer
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Apple introduced Apple Watch Series 12 with higher-frequency heart-rate and HRV sensing, a readiness score, and planned Audio Intelligence features including Live Rewind and Siri Recap.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product is positioned less as a sensor and more as an interpreter of personal context. The commercial work is making an unfamiliar intelligence layer feel useful in an existing daily ritual.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether readiness and memory features become repeated habits or remain launch-demo curiosities; the difference will show up in daily use, not announcement reach.

fieldNotes.title: Meta packages an agent as a general-purpose personal helper
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta introduced Muse, a personal AI agent that can act across connected apps, with a secure virtual machine, user-controlled permissions, audit trails, and confirmation for sensitive actions.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The pitch moves from answering questions to taking work off a person’s plate. That creates a much higher burden of trust, onboarding, and proof than a conversational feature requires.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch the first narrow, repeatable task that earns permission to act; broad claims about goals matter less than one workflow users willingly delegate twice.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI asks policy to move with capability
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI called for mandatory capability-based national AI safety requirements and announced support for four California bills covering infrastructure, auditor standards, youth protections, and biosecurity.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A product category that changes faster than public understanding eventually has to sell not only utility but a credible operating environment. Policy advocacy becomes part of the market-making effort.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether capability-based language produces specific, testable obligations or stays at the level of institutional positioning.

fieldNotes.title: AI agents create a new security bill for enterprise adoption
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reported that Cymphony raised $30 million to help companies control AI-agent access, after finding tens of thousands of corporate files exposed to AI tools and agents at one public company.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The adoption story is no longer only model quality or labor savings. Every agent that can move through company systems adds an access-control and observability cost that has to be priced into the result.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether security becomes a budgeted prerequisite for agent deployment or a retrofit after an incident; that timing will shape the category’s real sales cycle.

tweets.title: PlayStation ends PHYSINT collaboration with Kojima Productions
tweets.summary: PlayStation Studios announced that it is stepping away from collaborating with Kojima Productions on PHYSINT while describing the broader relationship as strong.
tweets.text: An update from PlayStation Studios: After careful consideration, we have made the difficult decision to step away from collaborating with KOJIMA PRODUCTIONS on its project PHYSINT. We continue to have great admiration for Hideo Kojima's vision for the game. Our relationship remains strong after three decades of industry-leading, genre-defining creative cooperation, and we look forward to continued close collaboration with Hideo Kojima and his award-winning independent studio in the future.
tweets.author: PlayStation

output.heading: Run one cost-to-result audit.
output.body: Choose one ambitious marketing effort. Name the behavior it must change, the cost of changing it, the result that would repay the work, and the earliest stop point if the evidence does not arrive.
